An [online search engine](https://www.google.co.uk/search?q=sample+contracts&oq=sample+contracts&aqs=chrome..69i57&sourceid=chrome&es_sm=122&ie=UTF-8) such as https://www.contractsuitable.com/search.php?term=employment%20clause shows 1.8m contract samples in total as a [JSON LD object](https://www.w3.org/TR/2014/REC-json-ld-20140116/#sec-linked-data).

The NLP techniques for entity extraction, sentence segmentation etc have improved recently, [this project](https://nlplt.cs.washington.edu/#sentececlassification) was built upon such developments, in conjunction with the [UMLS MetaThesaurus](https://www.nlm.nih.gov/research/umls/knowledge/Metathesaurus.shtml) to provide entity types (like "Solicitation of employees clause" from `Employee`, "Party type" from `Legal person`, "Employment period" from "Time of year"), semantic type (such as [`employment`](https://github.com/nlplt/uimaNlp/blob/431aef56da6e79d96562835a1a6da4bcf02c83b9/nltk.md#em), `"Ltd", "Inc", "LLC"`) or syntactic patterns for "disclaimer" and "terminations".

These entities were linked with their contextual information (i.e. their relation to the sentence). So to answer the questions about what clause/phrase each entity occurs in: they need a context (i.e. "context(clause1)=(part1, part2)" where claues are represented as [BuckHill nodes](https://www.nature.com/articles/nature20729.html)).

In a similar way to 1. above, one could try to identify patterns about whether a clause includes "solicitation" or "general advertisements" using a corpus of texts with relevant clauses and a NLP toolkit. It is a similar concept to sentence selection using a set of samples in a model (e.g. for sentiment analysis). The difficulty is to avoid a large biasing effect, although sample size shouldn't be relevant and there would be some unbiased cases in such "training set".

Clause 31 states:

"To ensure that a backup facility will be available in
case of such a failure..."

It doesn't restrict a party - it means that a party won't lose payments if the supplier can't meet their contractual terms. If the supplier can show it did everything the customer can require, they get paid. If the supplier does nothing the customer can reject everything and not owe the supplier anything - because the contract states they will have this backup. So if it can prevent some risk to the client, then the clause makes it very easy for the supplier to get paid and gives peace of mind in the client not having to pay if the supplier messes up. It also forces the supplier to do reasonable diligence in the relationship. It's a win-win in the supplier's (technical or administrative) perspective.

The comment on 'business interruption' could mean that it refers to 'business of interruption' only for a particular reason (think natural disaster - maybe the entire network and building infrastructure is in ruin but they keep paying for service for people in emergency needs or just in case the network needs to be up and live when they finally have all the power back, etc), not the entire company itself. Of course it could also mean all businesses are equally affected by one (natural disaster like fire etc. that burned the whole building) but in different ways - e.g. this is a business which is a cloud supplier for an insurance agency. So if they are affected and the fire comes to such a point - both of these companies will need to find another business to take care of their jobs, because they both burned up in a catastrophe. The former example makes the 'to make general searches for employees...' thing pointless if you think about it. So while it sounds like business 'interruption' would cause the need for both to fire their contractors, which then leads to both looking for replacement workers - that does not mean interruption in the business of each other. So both are allowed to 'solicit employees from the marketplace' and that might also happen as one (company) is looking to get rid of people, too. And it may (or may not) be in their power of decision to also fire people in the counterpartys group.
